svg.title: Separate a variant’s origin, inheritance and later selection
svg.desc: A somatic mutation can pass to daughter cells by mitosis but, when confined to that body-cell lineage, usually does not enter offspring through the germ line. A mutation in cells contributing to gametes may be inherited depending on which gamete contributes. Mutation creates new sequence variation; meiotic recombination primarily reshuffles existing variants. Neither origin nor inheritance proves a variant will increase in frequency: later reproductive contribution and environmental conditions matter. Mutations are not directed toward an organism’s anticipated need. Harmful,neutral or beneficial effects require a stated context and evidence across molecular,cellular and broader outcomes.

g.text: Separate a variant’s origin, inheritance and later selection
An original lineage comparison links C mechanisms to population reasoning in D.
Mutation creates a new sequence variant. Recombination reshuffles existing variants.
Origin of a variant → inheritance route → later changes in its population frequency.
Mutations do not arise in anticipation of future need. Selection acts on existing heritable variation.
A variant may have harmful, neutral or beneficial effects under particular conditions.
Sequence, expression, cell behaviour and broader outcomes each require their own evidence.
